note.explanation: At equilibrium, the forward and backward reactions continue at equal rates. The amounts of reactants and products stay constant, but the reactions have not stopped.
examples: For N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g), both sides have two moles of gas, so increasing pressure does not favour either direction.
For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), high pressure favours ammonia because the product side has fewer gas molecules.
note.checkAnswer: The concentrations of reactants and products stay constant because the forward and backward reaction rates are equal.
note.simple: Think of two equally fast streams of people moving in opposite directions. People are still moving, but the number on each side stays the same.
note.checkQuestion: At dynamic equilibrium, have the forward and backward reactions stopped?
note.title: Reversible Reactions and Equilibrium
steps: A reversible reaction can go in both the forward and backward directions.
In a closed system, the forward reaction starts and products begin to form.
As products build up, the backward reaction rate increases.
At equilibrium, forward and backward reaction rates are equal.
A change in temperature, pressure, or concentration can shift the equilibrium position.
note.answer: No. Both reactions continue, but at equal rates.

options: The equilibrium point will reach very soon.
The equilibrium point will reach very late.
The reaction will not attain the state of dynamic equilibrium.
The reaction will be practically irreversible.
mcqs.stem: Q6.1. What will happen if the rates of forward and reverse reactions are very high?
rationales: Correct: high forward and reverse rates allow equal rates to be reached quickly.
Incorrect: high reaction rates do not make equilibrium take longer to reach.
Incorrect: reversible reactions can attain dynamic equilibrium even when both rates are high.
Incorrect: high rates do not make a reversible reaction practically irreversible.

options: N₂ and H₂O
O₂ and H₂O
CO₂ and O₂
N₂ and O₂
mcqs.stem: Q6.2. Predict which components of the atmosphere react in the presence of lightning.
rationales: Incorrect: nitrogen and water are not the atmospheric components identified for this reaction.
Incorrect: oxygen and water are not the pair that reacts due to lightning in this example.
Incorrect: carbon dioxide and oxygen are not the pair that reacts due to lightning.
Correct: lightning provides energy for atmospheric nitrogen and oxygen to react.

options: Both the containers will have the same composition of mixtures.
Container A will have more concentration of PCl₃ than B.
Container A will have less concentration of PCl₃ than B.
Both the containers will have zero concentration of its reactants.
mcqs.stem: Q6.3. An inorganic chemist places one mole of PCl₃ in a container A and one mole of each Cl₂ and PCl₃ in container B. Both the containers were sealed and heated to the same temperature to reach the state of equilibrium. Guess about the composition of mixtures in both the containers.
rationales: Incorrect: the different starting mixtures do not produce identical equilibrium mixtures in these containers.
Correct: container B starts with Cl₂ as well as PCl₃, so more PCl₃ is used to form product than in A.
Incorrect: this reverses the expected comparison of the PCl₃ concentrations.
Incorrect: equilibrium does not normally use up all reactants.

options: Heating at high temperature in a closed vessel
Heating at high temperature in an open vessel
Cooling it in a closed vessel
Cooling it in an open vessel
mcqs.stem: Q6.4. CaO or lime is used extensively in steel, glass and paper industries. It is produced in an exothermic reversible reaction by the decomposition of lime (CaCO₃). Choose the conditions to produce maximum amount of lime.
rationales: Incorrect: a closed vessel allows CO₂ to build up, opposing further decomposition.
Correct: high temperature promotes decomposition, and an open vessel lets CO₂ escape.
Incorrect: cooling does not promote the decomposition needed to produce lime.
Incorrect: although CO₂ can escape, cooling does not favour decomposition.

options: All the reactants should be converted into the products.
50% of the reactants should be converted into products.
The concentrations of all the reactants and the products should become constant.
One of the products should be removed from the reaction mixture.
mcqs.stem: Q6.5. What condition should be met for the reversible reaction to achieve the state of equilibrium?
rationales: Incorrect: at equilibrium, some reactants usually remain.
Incorrect: equilibrium does not require exactly half of the reactants to be converted.
Correct: constant concentrations are a feature of equilibrium when the forward and backward rates are equal.
Incorrect: removing a product can shift equilibrium, but it is not a condition required to attain equilibrium.

options: Because the solubility of the gas increases
Because the gas is insoluble in water
Because the gas is dissolved under pressure hence it comes out when pressure is decreased
Because the solubility of the gas decreases at high pressure
mcqs.stem: Q6.6. Why the gas starts coming out when you open a can of fizzy drink?
rationales: Incorrect: decreasing pressure does not increase the gas's solubility in the drink.
Incorrect: the gas is dissolved in the drink before the can is opened.
Correct: opening the can lowers pressure, so dissolved gas escapes.
Incorrect: gas solubility increases, not decreases, when pressure is high.

options: The forward reaction will be favoured
The backward reaction will be favoured
No effect on backward reaction
No effect on forward or backward reaction
mcqs.stem:
Q6.7. The following reaction is performed in a closed vessel.

CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g)

How the equilibrium will be affected if you increase the pressure?
rationales: Incorrect: the forward side has more gas molecules, so higher pressure does not favour it.
Correct: the backward direction reduces the amount of gas and is favoured by increased pressure.
Incorrect: increased pressure affects the equilibrium direction in this reaction.
Incorrect: pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules, so it does have an effect.

options: If the activation energy of the forward reaction is comparable to that of backward reaction
If the activation energy of the forward reaction is higher than that of backward reaction
If the activation energy of the forward reaction is lower than that of backward reaction
If the enthalpy change of both the reactions is zero.
mcqs.stem: Q6.8. When a reaction will become a reversible one?
rationales: Correct: comparable activation energies make the forward and backward processes possible under suitable conditions.
Incorrect: a higher forward activation energy alone is not the stated condition for reversibility.
Incorrect: a lower forward activation energy alone is not the stated condition for reversibility.
Incorrect: zero enthalpy change is not a requirement for a reaction to be reversible.

options: No
Yes
They are useful only when equilibrium lies far to the right side
They are useful only when equilibrium lies far to the left side
mcqs.stem: Q6.9. Is reversible reaction useful for preparing compounds on large scale?
rationales: Incorrect: reversible reactions can be used in large-scale preparation.
Incorrect: this is too broad; usefulness depends on the equilibrium yield and conditions.
Correct: a reaction with equilibrium far to the product side can give a useful product yield.
Incorrect: equilibrium far to the reactant side gives little product.

options: They will remain constant
They will keep on increasing
They will keep on decreasing
They will remain constant for some time and then start decreasing
mcqs.stem: Q6.10. What will happen to the concentrations of the products if a reversible reaction at equilibrium is not disturbed?
rationales: Correct: at undisturbed equilibrium the forward and backward rates are equal, so product concentrations remain constant.
Incorrect: products do not keep accumulating at equilibrium.
Incorrect: products are not continually consumed overall at equilibrium.
Incorrect: if the system remains undisturbed, the equilibrium concentrations remain constant.

written.text: How is dynamic equilibrium different from the static equilibrium?
written.finalAnswer: Dynamic equilibrium has ongoing forward and backward reactions at equal rates; static equilibrium has no ongoing change or movement.

rubric.why: This identifies what continues in dynamic equilibrium.
rubric.description: State that forward and backward reactions continue at equal rates.
rubric.how: Mention both continuing reactions and equal rates.

rubric.why: This distinguishes static equilibrium from dynamic equilibrium.
rubric.description: State that static equilibrium has no ongoing reaction or movement.
rubric.how: Contrast dynamic activity with no ongoing change.

modelAnswer: In dynamic equilibrium, the forward and backward reactions continue at equal rates.
In static equilibrium, there is no ongoing reaction or movement.

written.text:
How the following reversible reaction will be affected if its temperature is increased?

Electricity

2H₂O(l) ⇌ 2H₂(g) + O₂(g)
written.finalAnswer: Increasing temperature favours the forward, endothermic direction, producing more H₂ and O₂.

rubric.why: The direction favoured by added heat must be identified.
rubric.description: Explain that added heat favours the endothermic direction.
rubric.how: Name the forward direction and relate it to heat absorption.

rubric.why: The answer should state the effect on the products.
rubric.description: State that more hydrogen and oxygen are formed.
rubric.how: Identify both gaseous products.

modelAnswer: The forward decomposition of water is endothermic.
On increasing temperature, the forward reaction is favoured.
The amounts of H₂ and O₂ increase.

written.text: How can you get the maximum yield in a reversible reaction?
written.finalAnswer: Choose conditions that shift equilibrium towards products: use a suitable temperature and pressure, increase reactant concentration, and remove products as they form.

rubric.why: Maximum yield requires equilibrium to favour product formation.
rubric.description: State that conditions should favour the forward reaction.
rubric.how: Refer to shifting equilibrium towards the products.

rubric.why: Give a practical way of adjusting the equilibrium position.
rubric.description: Name suitable changes such as removing product or adjusting pressure, temperature, or concentration.
rubric.how: Give at least one relevant condition or product-removal method.

modelAnswer: Select suitable temperature and pressure conditions to favour the forward reaction.
Increase the concentration of reactants or remove products as they form.
These changes shift the equilibrium towards the products and increase the yield.

written.text: How can you decrease the time to attain the position of equilibrium in a reversible reaction?
written.finalAnswer: Use a catalyst to increase the forward and backward reaction rates; equilibrium is reached sooner without changing its position.

rubric.why: A catalyst is the standard way to make equilibrium be reached sooner.
rubric.description: Name a catalyst.
rubric.how: State that a catalyst is added.

rubric.why: The explanation must show that both directions are sped up without shifting equilibrium.
rubric.description: Explain that both reaction rates increase and equilibrium is reached sooner.
rubric.how: Mention both directions or both rates.

modelAnswer: Add a catalyst to the reaction mixture.
The catalyst increases the rates of both forward and backward reactions.
The equilibrium position is reached sooner, but its position does not change.

written.text:
What is the effect of increasing pressure on the following reaction at equilibrium?

N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g)
written.finalAnswer: There is no effect on the equilibrium position because both sides have two moles of gas.

rubric.why: The equilibrium shift must be stated.
rubric.description: State that pressure has no effect on the equilibrium position.
rubric.how: Clearly state that neither direction is favoured.

rubric.why: Equal gas amounts on both sides explain the result.
rubric.description: Compare the total gaseous moles on each side.
rubric.how: State that each side has two moles of gas.

modelAnswer: The reactant side has 2 moles of gas: 1 mole N₂ + 1 mole O₂.
The product side has 2 moles of gas: 2 moles NO.
Increasing pressure has no effect on the equilibrium position.

written.text: Why are some reactions irreversible while others are reversible?
written.finalAnswer: Some reactions are reversible because their products can react to reform the reactants under suitable conditions; others are effectively irreversible because the reverse reaction does not occur appreciably or products escape or become stable.

rubric.why: This describes the defining possibility in a reversible reaction.
rubric.description: Explain that products can react back to form reactants.
rubric.how: Mention a backward reaction under suitable conditions.

rubric.why: This distinguishes reactions whose reverse is negligible or hindered.
rubric.description: Explain why some reactions proceed effectively only forward.
rubric.how: Mention negligible reverse reaction, escaping products, or stable products.

modelAnswer: A reaction is reversible when its products can react to form the original reactants under suitable conditions.
Some reactions are effectively irreversible because the reverse reaction is negligible, or because products escape or are very stable.

written.text: Why are combustion reactions generally irreversible?
written.finalAnswer: Combustion forms stable products and releases energy; the products do not readily react back to the original fuel and oxygen.

rubric.why: Stable products help explain why the reverse reaction is not readily observed.
rubric.description: State that combustion forms stable products.
rubric.how: Use the idea of stable products.

rubric.why: This explains why combustion generally does not reverse under ordinary conditions.
rubric.description: State that products do not readily reform fuel and oxygen.
rubric.how: Describe the reverse reaction as not readily occurring.

modelAnswer: Combustion forms stable products and releases energy.
These products do not readily react back to form the original fuel and oxygen, so combustion is generally irreversible.

written.text: How do you know if a reaction is reversible or irreversible?
written.finalAnswer: A reversible reaction can proceed in both directions, with products reforming reactants; an irreversible reaction proceeds effectively in one direction under the stated conditions.

rubric.why: The possibility of a backward reaction identifies reversibility.
rubric.description: Describe a reversible reaction as proceeding in both directions.
rubric.how: Mention products reforming reactants.

rubric.why: This provides the contrast needed to identify an irreversible reaction.
rubric.description: Describe an irreversible reaction as proceeding effectively in one direction.
rubric.how: State that a significant backward reaction does not occur.

modelAnswer: A reversible reaction proceeds in both forward and backward directions, so products can reform reactants.
An irreversible reaction proceeds effectively in one direction under the stated conditions.

written.text: Do the phase changes in water (solid to liquid, liquid to vapour) reversible or irreversible?
written.finalAnswer: They are reversible: ice can melt and water can freeze, while liquid water can evaporate and water vapour can condense.

rubric.why: The answer must classify the phase changes.
rubric.description: State that the phase changes are reversible.
rubric.how: Use the word reversible.

rubric.why: Reverse phase changes support the classification.
rubric.description: Give at least one pair of opposite changes.
rubric.how: Name melting/freezing or evaporation/condensation.

modelAnswer: The phase changes in water are reversible.
Ice melts to liquid water, and liquid water freezes to ice.
Liquid water evaporates to vapour, and vapour condenses to liquid water.

written.text:
How can you drive the reversible reaction at equilibrium?

(a) in the forward direction  
(b) in the backward direction
written.finalAnswer: Change conditions to favour the forward reaction for (a), or favour the backward reaction for (b), by adjusting concentration, pressure, or temperature as appropriate.

rubric.why: The forward change must shift equilibrium towards products.
rubric.description: Give a condition that favours the forward direction.
rubric.how: For example, increase reactant concentration or remove product.

rubric.why: The backward change must shift equilibrium towards reactants.
rubric.description: Give a condition that favours the backward direction.
rubric.how: For example, increase product concentration or remove reactant.

modelAnswer: (a) Increase the concentration of a reactant or remove a product to drive the reaction forward.
(b) Increase the concentration of a product or remove a reactant to drive the reaction backward.
Pressure and temperature can also be changed when they favour the required direction.

written.text: Explain how the rates of forward and backward reactions change when the system approaches equilibrium.
written.finalAnswer: The forward rate decreases and the backward rate increases as equilibrium is approached; at equilibrium the rates are equal.

rubric.why: The change in forward rate must be described.
rubric.description: State that the forward rate decreases as reactants are used.
rubric.how: Describe the forward reaction as slowing.

rubric.why: The increasing reverse rate and equality at equilibrium complete the explanation.
rubric.description: State that the backward rate increases until it equals the forward rate.
rubric.how: Mention both increasing backward rate and equal rates at equilibrium.

modelAnswer: As reactants are used up, the rate of the forward reaction decreases.
As products form, the rate of the backward reaction increases.
At equilibrium, the two rates become equal and the concentrations remain constant.

written.text: Describe the effect of a catalyst on the reversible reaction.
written.finalAnswer: A catalyst increases both forward and backward reaction rates, so equilibrium is reached sooner, but the equilibrium position and yield are unchanged.

rubric.why: A catalyst acts on both directions of a reversible reaction.
rubric.description: State that it increases both reaction rates.
rubric.how: Mention both forward and backward reactions.

rubric.why: The answer must distinguish reaction speed from equilibrium position.
rubric.description: State that equilibrium is reached sooner but its position does not change.
rubric.how: Include both effects.

modelAnswer: A catalyst increases the rates of both the forward and backward reactions.
The system reaches equilibrium sooner.
The catalyst does not change the equilibrium position or the equilibrium yield.

written.text: Study the effect of heat on hydrated copper sulphate. Why does this salt look coloured and why does it lose colour upon heating?
written.finalAnswer: Hydrated copper sulphate is blue because of its water of crystallisation. Heating removes this water, forming white anhydrous copper sulphate; adding water restores the blue colour.

rubric.why: This explains the original colour of hydrated copper sulphate.
rubric.description: Identify the hydrated salt as blue and relate it to water of crystallisation.
rubric.how: State the colour and the role of hydration.

rubric.why: Heating removes the water responsible for hydration.
rubric.description: Explain what heating does to the hydrated salt.
rubric.how: Say that it loses water of crystallisation.

rubric.why: The product and its observed colour must be identified.
rubric.description: Name the white anhydrous product.
rubric.how: State that anhydrous copper sulphate is white.

rubric.why: Rehydration demonstrates the reversible colour change.
rubric.description: State that adding water restores the blue colour.
rubric.how: Describe the colour returning after water is added.

modelAnswer: Hydrated copper sulphate is blue because it contains water of crystallisation.
On heating, it loses water and forms anhydrous copper sulphate.
Anhydrous copper sulphate is white, so the salt loses its blue colour.
Adding water to the anhydrous salt restores the blue colour.

written.text: Synthesis of ammonia gas is very important industrially because it is used in the preparation of urea fertilizer. Explain the conditions you will use to get the maximum yield of ammonia.
written.finalAnswer: Use nitrogen and hydrogen in a 1:3 ratio, high pressure, a moderate temperature of about 450°C, and an iron catalyst; remove ammonia as it forms. These conditions give a high practical yield.

rubric.why: Correct reactant proportions support ammonia synthesis.
rubric.description: Give the nitrogen-to-hydrogen ratio.
rubric.how: State one part nitrogen to three parts hydrogen.

rubric.why: High pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules.
rubric.description: State that high pressure favours ammonia formation.
rubric.how: Link increased pressure to the product side.

rubric.why: The moderate temperature gives a practical balance of yield and reaction rate.
rubric.description: Give the moderate operating temperature, about 450°C.
rubric.how: State about 450°C or identify a moderate temperature.

rubric.why: The catalyst helps the process reach equilibrium faster.
rubric.description: Name the iron catalyst.
rubric.how: State that iron is used as a catalyst.

rubric.why: Removing product shifts equilibrium towards further ammonia formation.
rubric.description: State that ammonia is removed as it forms.
rubric.how: Explain that removing product promotes the forward reaction.

modelAnswer: The reaction is N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g).
Use nitrogen and hydrogen in a 1:3 ratio.
Use high pressure because the product side has fewer gas molecules.
Use a moderate temperature of about 450°C and an iron catalyst.
Remove ammonia as it forms to shift the equilibrium towards further product formation.

examTips: Short questions often ask for the difference between dynamic and static equilibrium, or the effect of changing pressure, temperature, or concentration.
For a pressure question, count only gaseous moles on each side; ignore solids and liquids.
For a temperature question, identify which direction is endothermic and state which direction added heat favours.
For a catalyst question, earn marks by stating that both reaction rates increase, equilibrium is reached sooner, and the equilibrium position is unchanged.
In descriptive answers, explain the condition and its effect on the equilibrium position; do not just name a condition.

hints: Compare the total moles of gas on the left and right.
Count N₂ and O₂ as two gas moles on the left and 2NO as two on the right.
yourTurn.question:
What is the effect of increasing pressure on the following reaction at equilibrium?

N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g)
solution: The left side has 1 mole N₂ + 1 mole O₂ = 2 moles of gas.
The right side has 2 moles of NO = 2 moles of gas.
Both sides have the same number of gas moles.
Increasing pressure has no effect on the equilibrium position.
yourTurn.answer: There is no effect on the equilibrium position.

hints: A catalyst affects the speed of a reaction.
Remember that it affects both directions and does not shift equilibrium.
yourTurn.question: Describe the effect of a catalyst on the reversible reaction.
solution: A catalyst increases the rates of both the forward and backward reactions.
The catalyst does not change the equilibrium position or yield.
yourTurn.answer: A catalyst speeds up both reactions so equilibrium is reached sooner, but it does not change the equilibrium position.

steps.why: Writing the balanced reversible equation identifies the reactants, product, and gas amounts.
The product side has fewer gas molecules, so pressure is an important condition for shifting the equilibrium.
steps.text: Compare gaseous moles: left side = 1 + 3 = 4; right side = 2.

steps.why: High pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules.
steps.text: Use high pressure to favour the forward reaction and increase NH₃ formation.

steps.why: A moderate temperature and catalyst help the industrial reaction proceed at a useful rate and yield.
steps.text: Use about 450°C and an iron catalyst.

steps.why: Removing product shifts equilibrium towards forming more product.

example.question: Synthesis of ammonia gas is very important industrially because it is used in the preparation of urea fertilizer. Explain the conditions you will use to get the maximum yield of ammonia.
example.answer: Use N₂ and H₂ in a 1:3 ratio, high pressure, about 450°C, and an iron catalyst; remove NH₃ as it forms.

explain.title: Reversible reactions
explain.body: A reversible reaction can proceed in the forward and backward directions. The symbol ⇌ shows that both directions are possible.

explain.title: Dynamic equilibrium
explain.body: In a closed system, equilibrium is reached when the forward and backward reaction rates are equal. Both reactions continue, but the concentrations stay constant.

explain.title: Changing equilibrium
explain.body: Changing concentration, pressure, or temperature can favour one direction. The system responds by shifting in the direction that reduces the effect of the change.

explain.title: Pressure and temperature
explain.body: Increased pressure favours the side with fewer moles of gas. Increased temperature favours the endothermic direction; cooling favours the exothermic direction.

explain.title: Catalysts
explain.body: A catalyst speeds up both forward and backward reactions. It helps equilibrium be reached sooner, but does not change the equilibrium position or yield.

mistakes: Do not say that the reactions stop at dynamic equilibrium; they continue at equal rates.
Do not count solids or liquids when comparing gaseous moles for pressure effects.
Do not claim that a catalyst shifts equilibrium or increases the equilibrium yield.
Do not say that every reversible reaction produces equal amounts of reactants and products.
For temperature changes, do not forget to identify which direction is endothermic.
